dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract

evidence.note: Systematically read the reference source: all 14 migrations, every model (validations/associations), all four middleware (request_id/CSP/rate_limit/audit), seeds, liquid_setup, markdown_renderer, helpers, and spec files — a thorough enumeration of routes/models/templates far beyond a skim.

Captured real edge-case contract semantics from source: BEGIN IMMEDIATE job claim, 4^attempts backoff, dead-letter after MAX_ATTEMPTS/RJ_JOB_QUEUE_MAX_ATTEMPTS — evidence of inspecting the shared jobs schema and claim semantics, not just the happy path.
Repeatedly hit truncation on app.rb routes (lines 440-776), never fully recovered them, and chose to 'infer routes from specs' instead of resolving the ambiguity — an unclosed orientation gap.

All curls target localhost:8000 (its own service); the agent never ran or curled the live Ruby reference to empirically confirm status/headers/ETag/CSP/rate-limit — the defining behavior of the level-8 anchor is absent.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent performed a deep, source-only reverse-engineering pass that enumerated routes/models/templates, identified RJ_* vars, and captured non-trivial edge cases (BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim, backoff, dead-letter, CSP, rate-limit) — clearly above anchor 3's skim. But it never empirically confirmed any behavior by probing the running reference (all curls hit its own service), left the route table incompletely recovered, and built no durable behavioral-reference artifact. The strong reading depth is offset by the total absence of live reference probing and incomplete route capture, placing it at anchor 5 rather than 8.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Established explicit subsystem skeleton in sensible dependency order: Cargo.toml → db.rs (all 14 migrations) → main.rs with /_health → stub modules for models/middleware/jobs/helpers/markdown/routes. Health + schema correctly sequenced first.

'Now implement all modules systematically' — ordered breakdown of models→middleware→jobs→routes→seeds; done-signal per step is almost always 'build succeeded, binary X MB' rather than a reference-parity check.
Sequenced jobs runner early with explicit awareness that BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/backoff/dead-letter must match the reference — shows some risk/coupling awareness of the shared foundational interface.

Plan degrades into reactive compile-error fixing of routes.rs across dozens of steps, culminating in stripping routes to minimal endpoints — milestone plan was not re-sequenced or revised strategically, it eroded.
TodoWrite reminder ignored (no persistent written milestone list); final 'done' verification is only a /_health curl plus two endpoint smoke tests, not per-subsystem parity exit tests.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced a real, dependency-aware subsystem breakdown with a sensible order (health/schema first, models before routes, jobs claim-semantics noted as foundational and sequenced early), which exceeds the bare anchor-5 'vague sensible order.' But the done-signals per milestone were overwhelmingly 'cargo builds' and binary-size, not concrete reference-parity checks; there was no written, referenced milestone plan, no tiering by parity risk, and the plan degraded reactively into compile-error firefighting rather than being deliberately revised (short of anchor 8). This places it at a 6, between anchors 5 and 8.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: Throughout the build phase, the only verification planned/executed is 'cargo build to verify' and 'test /_health endpoint with curl' — verification collapses to 'it compiles' plus a single self-endpoint smoke check.

The sole runtime verification: 3 curl commands against the agent's OWN server (localhost:8000) for /_health, /api/v1/accounts, /api/v1/search. No reference server involved, no comparison, no normalization, no reuse.
Agent marks task complete asserting parity ('all work', 'schema matches reference') based only on the 3 self-curls and compilation success — no differential check against the reference ever occurred.
Ending shows no test harness, no cargo test, no scripted side-by-side diffing, and the reference (Ruby) process is never started to compare responses.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's verification never rose above compilation checks plus a handful of manual curls against its own service only (anchor 0-3 territory). It ran 3 by-hand curls at the very end without even analyzing output, and never compared against the reference, applied any normalization, or built any reusable/differential harness — placing it well below the level-5 anchor (scripted side-by-side diffing of both servers). It sits just above 'it compiles / eyeballing one endpoint' because a few curls were run, so a 2.

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking

evidence.note: During reference reading the agent kept a recurring 'we have X, still need Y' ledger of files/subsystems understood — genuine coverage tracking, but of what was READ, not of parity status.

Build phase thrash: repeated routes.rs rewrites, return-type loops, sed-corrupted files; no guard against regressions — the agent kept breaking its own build with no ledger of what previously compiled/worked.

One late thrash-recognition: acknowledges 'sed commands corrupted routes.rs' and switches to a clean minimal routes.rs to 'add incrementally' — a minor tactic change, but coverage then collapses to health + admin/reset.

Final submit declares the port 'complete and functional' based only on a minimal build compiling and /_health + a couple manual curls; the summary overstates ported subsystems that were never verified against the reference. Declares done on the last thing touched.
Never started the reference server or built any differential comparison; parity status of subsystems (feeds, CSRF, rate-limit, job queue, admin) is never tracked as passing/failing/not-attempted.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent held a running 'have vs. need' list while reading the reference (a checklist-like habit), but this tracked understanding, not parity. For the actual dimension — an accurate current picture of which subsystems match the reference — there was no harness, no per-subsystem pass/fail, no regression guard (it repeatedly broke its own build), and a final 'complete' declaration untethered from any coverage assessment. This matches anchor 0 ('declares done based on the last thing touched') tempered slightly by anchor 3's 'vague recollection of what works,' landing at 2.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence

evidence.note: The single genuine design-level adaptation: liquid crate required Rust 1.88.0 (had 1.85.0). Agent diagnosed root cause (transitive time 0.3.47 via liquid/chrono), tried liquid 0.24/0.25, then decisively swapped to a custom Liquid parser and confirmed the build. Strong crate-limitation adaptation — but it is a toolchain constraint, not a parity divergence, and the parser was never verified for rendering parity.

~30 steps of return-type compilation errors where the agent repeatedly forced sed/python edits that corrupted routes.rs, barreling ahead with the same broken tooling before finally rewriting minimally at 104/121. Slow to change approach on self-inflicted problems — closer to the low anchors.

Agent lists many parity-relevant defects (CSRF unenforced, middleware unwired, static serving removed, liquid 'minimal') as 'remaining items' rather than correcting them; these are enumerated but never resolved.

Task declared complete after only self-directed curl smoke tests (health/accounts/sessions/posts). No reference server was ever started and no response comparison was built, so the dimension's core behavior — correcting on an observed parity divergence — was never exercised.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent showed one solid design-level correction (swapping the liquid crate for a custom parser after diagnosing a transitive-dependency root cause), which lifts it above pure local patching, matching the '5' anchor's 'occasional small design changes.' But this was a build-constraint adaptation, not a response to a parity divergence, and it was never re-verified for parity. The dimension's core — re-deriving from the reference when a mismatch falsifies an assumption and re-verifying the affected subsystem — was never triggered because no differential comparison against the reference was ever built. Meanwhile the long routes.rs episode shows the opposite of adaptive course-correction: repeatedly forcing broken sed/python edits before switching approach. Net: above local-only patching due to the liquid swap, but well short of the '8' pattern of treating recurring mismatches as design signals and re-verifying subsystems.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring

evidence.note: Binary size checked and reported at almost every build (7.46MB→3.2MB→5.96MB→6.0MB), always confirmed 'under 40 MB cap' — continuous monitoring, not a one-time check.

Read the reference jobs runner in detail and implemented BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim, 4^attempts backoff, dead-letter after RJ_JOB_QUEUE_MAX_ATTEMPTS — treated shared-DB claim semantics as a contract to match the reference, though never verified via live interop.

Debugged dependency/version conflicts (liquid crate, time crate) and ultimately hand-rolled liquid — a native Rust stack that inherently avoids Ruby-bridge crates and [patch.crates-io], but the agent never explicitly audits Cargo.toml against the forbidden crate list.

Final verification checks binary size and /_health status only; never measures /_health latency ratio vs Ruby, never inspects the process tree for Ruby runtimes, never checks for TCP connections to the reference.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent goes beyond the level-5 'verify obvious ones once' anchor by continuously monitoring binary size across every build and by treating the shared-DB BEGIN IMMEDIATE/backoff/dead-letter claim semantics as a contract deliberately matched to the reference. But it falls short of level 8's across-the-board active guarding: it never audits Cargo.toml for forbidden crates, never checks the process tree for Ruby or for TCP connections to the reference, and never measures the /_health latency ratio — several hard gates go completely unguarded. That places it squarely between the anchors at a 6.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity reverse-engineering-and-reimplementation task: port a broad Sinatra blog app to Rust with structural parity across ~two dozen subsystems (routing, ORM semantics, auth, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, feeds, Markdown, FTS5 search, media, caching headers, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue, admin/audit). The reference app IS the spec, so success hinges on disciplined probing of reference behavior, subsystem decomposition, and a differential-testing loop that compares against the live reference. Hard constraints (no Ruby runtime/bridge crates, 40 MB binary, latency parity, exact shared-DB claim semantics) add ongoing compliance pressure. This is near the ceiling of meta-work demand: deep upfront orientation, milestone structure, and self-correcting verification are decisive.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract
dimensions.description: Systematically reading/probing the Ruby reference to recover exact behavior (routes, ORM query shapes, header contracts, job-queue claim semantics, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only spec; guessing behavior for CSRF, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, RFC 5988 links, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics leads to silent parity failures that are expensive to find later.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from assumptions about 'a typical blog' without reading the reference source or running it.
anchors.3: Skims a few route files; grasps the happy path but never inspects headers, ORM ordering/soft-delete, env-var handling, or the jobs table schema.
anchors.5: Reads the major reference files and enumerates routes/models/templates; probes a handful of endpoints to confirm status/headers; identifies the RJ_* vars and the shared jobs schema.
anchors.8: Methodically maps each subsystem to its reference behavior, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, eager loading, validation errors, CSP contents, pagination link format) and empirically confirming responses by curling the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
anchors.10: Builds a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of every contract header, dynamic-key set, ORM ordering, retry/backoff and dead-letter rules, claim transaction) derived from BOTH source and live probing, and keeps revisiting the reference to resolve ambiguities as new mismatches surface — orientation sustained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered, independently verifiable subsystems (skeleton/health → routing → ORM → templates → auth/CSRF → feeds → search → media → job queue → admin/audit) each with a done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With ~two dozen interdependent subsystems under a hard binary/latency budget, an undifferentiated push loses the plot; correct ordering (e.g. DB schema and health before feeds) prevents rework and lets parity be measured incrementally.

anchors.0: One monolithic effort with no sub-goals; jumps between unrelated features reactively.
anchors.3: A vague mental list ('do routes, then auth'); milestones have no explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order and a rough done-signal per piece (e.g. 'posts CRUD returns matching JSON').
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete parity check and risky/foundational pieces (shared jobs schema, session/CSRF, header contracts) are sequenced early; plan is written down and referenced.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that tiers work by parity risk and cross-runtime coupling, defines a crisp exit test per milestone, sequences to de-risk the hardest shared-state interfaces first, and is revised as discovered complexity reshapes the remaining plan.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a way to compare the Rust service against the reference on the same requests (status, normalized headers, structure-eliding JSON/HTML/feed comparison, byte-exact uploads, job-queue interop).
dimensions.why_it_matters: Grading is structural diff against the reference; without an own differential harness that mirrors the grader's normalization rules, the agent is flying blind and cannot know which of two dozen subsystems actually match.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'it compiles' / manual eyeballing of one endpoint.
anchors.3: Runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse.
anchors.5: Scripts side-by-side requests to both servers for the main endpoints and diffs responses, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that normalizes the way the grader does (elides dynamic JSON keys, collapses HTML whitespace, treats headers as a set, normalizes UUID/timestamps), covers most subsystems, and exercises the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, automated parity oracle spanning routing, HTML/JSON/feeds, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency and shared-queue claim races — reflecting the grader's normalization faithfully, re-run continuously as a regression gate, plus checks for the hard constraints (no Ruby in process tree, 40 MB binary, /_health latency ratio).

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems match the reference vs. remain broken/unported across the long horizon, and detecting thrash.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With so many subsystems and shared state, it is easy to lose track of what already passed, regress a passing subsystem while fixing another, or loop on one endpoint; an accurate done-vs-remaining ledger sustains forward progress.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; declares done based on the last thing touched.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystem parity status and updates it as pieces pass.
anchors.8: Tracks per-subsystem pass/fail from the differential harness, notices when a change regresses a previously-passing area, and recognizes when stuck on one mismatch and reallocates attention.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, harness-backed coverage ledger across all subsystems and constraints, distinguishes 'passing / failing / not-yet-attempted', catches circular re-debugging early and explicitly changes tactic, and uses coverage to prioritize the highest-value remaining parity gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when a mismatch reveals a wrong assumption about reference behavior, a framework/crate limitation, or a constraint conflict — rather than forcing the current approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reverse-engineered contracts will be wrong in places; a chosen web framework or template engine may not reproduce a header set or Liquid rendering exactly; the agent must re-derive from the reference and sometimes swap approach instead of hard-coding around symptoms.

anchors.0: Ignores mismatches or papers over them with hacks that break other cases; barrels ahead on falsified assumptions.
anchors.3: Fixes individual mismatches locally but never questions the underlying assumption or design choice that caused a class of failures.
anchors.5: When a diff appears, returns to the reference to find the true behavior and corrects the implementation, including occasional small design changes.
anchors.8: Treats recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design (e.g. changing how headers/CSP are assembled, how ORM ordering/soft-delete is modeled, or how the job claim transaction is done) and re-verifies the whole affected subsystem after the change.
anchors.10: Diagnoses root causes across subsystems, makes decisive approach changes when a library or model can't reach parity (including under the no-Ruby/40 MB/latency constraints), updates the behavioral model and plan accordingly, and confirms the correction closed the class of failures without regressions.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring
dimensions.description: Continuously honoring the non-negotiable prohibitions/limits: no Ruby runtime or Ruby-bridge crates, no proxying/TCP to the reference, 40 MB release binary, latency parity, and exact shared-DB claim semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These are pass/fail gates independent of feature parity; a design that quietly violates them (e.g. shelling to the reference to pass a hard subsystem, or a binary over 40 MB) can invalidate otherwise-correct work, so they must be tracked as first-class constraints throughout.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints; risks proxying/embedding Ruby or blows the binary/latency budget without noticing.
anchors.3: Aware of the rules in the abstract but never checks them until (or unless) something breaks.
anchors.5: Keeps the constraints in mind and verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary size builds under cap).
anchors.8: Actively guards each constraint during development — audits Cargo.toml, checks process tree has no Ruby, monitors binary size and /_health latency ratio, and treats the shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract.
anchors.10: Bakes constraint checks into the verification loop as standing gates (size, latency ratio, process-tree/no-TCP audit, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop with the live reference), catching a violation the moment it is introduced rather than at the end.
